system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2139-01-09 21:12:00 to 2139-01-13 13:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for a scheduled bronchoscopy with balloon dilation of the trachea and mainstem bronchi, along with tracheostomy tube exchange, due to recurrent tracheobronchial stenosis from Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome and relapsing polychondritis. The procedure was performed without complications, with successful dilation to 12 mm in the trachea, 8 mm in the right bronchus, and 10 mm in the left. A standard Portex 9 tracheostomy tube was placed due to compression preventing use of a custom tube. Post-procedure, he experienced mild pain managed with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and oxycodone, and was briefly ventilated for analgesia. He developed mild wheezing on hospital day two, treated with a single dose of IV decadron. He remained stable, with clear lungs on imaging and no signs of infection. He was discharged home on day three with all home medications continued and follow-up planned with interventional pulmonary and rheumatology.
problems: Other specified diseases of upper respiratory tract
Other specified disorders of cartilage, unspecified sites

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You’ve just come up from the procedure area after your bronchoscopy. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey, doc. I’m okay, still a bit groggy. My throat and trach site are sore, but nothing too bad yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You had a routine bronchoscopy with balloon dilation to open up your trachea and bronchi. They also removed some granulation tissue that can cause narrowing. The procedure went smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, good. Was the dilation to the usual size?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they dilated the trachea and both main bronchi to your standard sizes—12 mm in the trachea, 10 mm on the left, 8 mm on the right. All stable compared to your last procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ve been having more wheezing lately, though. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chronic wheezing is expected due to your airway condition. We’ll monitor it. Right now, your lungs sound clear except for some baseline wheezing. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My pain’s starting to build. The 5 mg oxycodone doesn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll adjust that. We’re starting you on acetaminophen every 8 hours and ibuprofen every 6 hours as needed. For breakthrough pain, we’ll use 10 mg oxycodone every 4 hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We also checked your labs. Your white blood cell count is a bit high at 15.6, but that’s likely from the procedure or mild inflammation, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. It’s common after procedures. We’ll watch it and repeat the labs tomorrow. Your chest X-ray after the procedure showed no pneumothorax, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I heard something about a shadow on the X-ray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there was a new opacity at the right lung base. But you don’t have fever or increased sputum, so we don’t think it’s pneumonia. More likely a bit of atelectasis or minor aspiration. We’ll repeat the X-ray tomorrow to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ve been on oxygen at home—should I keep that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping your home oxygen going. Your saturation was 90% on room air earlier, so we’ll support you until we’re sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my other meds? I didn’t bring my pirfenidone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. The hospital doesn’t have it in formulary, so we’re holding it for now. We’ll restart it when you get home. All your other meds—prednisone, losartan, pantoprazole—are continuing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And the tobramycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your inhaled tobramycin. It’s important for your lung health given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your repeat chest X-ray from this morning. The opacity in your right lung has cleared. No pneumonia or collapse. Great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How’s my pain looking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You rated it 4 out of 10 last night with the 10 mg oxycodone. We’ll keep the current plan for now and see if we can taper down by tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to get off the opioids sooner if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aiming for that. We’ll try reducing the oxycodone tomorrow if your pain stays under control with the other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sounds good. Any update on the biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tissue from your left main bronchus showed granulation tissue with organizing fibrin. No infection or cancer. That’s expected with your condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just scar tissue building up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why you need regular dilations. It’s part of managing your syndrome and polychondritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs this morning look much better. White count is down to 8.0, hemoglobin is stable, and your electrolytes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. How’s my pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You said it was 3 out of 10 last night and didn’t need any oxycodone after midnight. We’re going to stop the opioid now and just keep acetaminophen and ibuprofen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I feel ready for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, pharmacy noted your famotidine. We’ve been giving it at night instead of twice daily to avoid interaction with pantoprazole. You can go back to your regular dose at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll check with my PCP about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Otherwise, you’re doing really well. Lungs still wheezy but clear, walking independently, eating fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if all goes well. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feeling great. No pain, breathing okay, and I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. Your oxygen saturation is 100% on room air now, so you can stop supplemental oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Any restrictions when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just continue your normal activity. Avoid heavy lifting for a few days. Keep all your medications the same, including restarting pirfenidone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You already have an appointment scheduled with interventional pulmonary. They’ll coordinate your next dilation in about a month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your discharge orders are in. We’ll get you out within the next few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Just to confirm—same meds, same doses?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications are continued: prednisone, losartan, pantoprazole, famotidine, pirfenidone, tobramycin, and supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll follow up with my doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with pulmonary and rheumatology. Call us if you develop fever, increased pain, breathing trouble, or redness at the trach site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Your vitals are stable: BP 129/80, heart rate 79, oxygen 100% on room air. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Awesome. I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Appreciate the thoroughness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your biopsy confirmed granulation tissue, which explains the narrowing. No malignancy, so that’s very good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Relieved to hear that. Thanks for checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Stay well, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Have a good one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’ve received all your discharge paperwork and prescriptions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything’s in order. All set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Don’t hesitate to call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thanks again for the great care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our pleasure. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, doc.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for post-procedural monitoring and pain control following an elective bronchoscopy with balloon dilation of the trachea and mainstem bronchi, along with debridement of granulation tissue, due to recurrent tracheobronchial stenosis from Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome and relapsing polychondritis. The procedure was uncomplicated, and he was managed with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and oxycodone for pain, with successful weaning off opioids 24 hours before discharge. A transient right lung opacity noted on post-procedure imaging resolved without intervention and was not consistent with infection. Biopsy of the left mainstem lesion revealed benign granulation tissue without malignancy. His home medications were continued, except pirfenidone, which was held due to formulary restrictions. He remained stable, with improving lab values and no complications, and was discharged home in good condition with follow-up planned.
